rv.q: This timely revival, reminding a 2022 audience of the consequence of dreadful compromise, is anchored by a behemoth of a lead performance by David Tennant, who proves once more what a magnetic stage presence he is.
It’s a grim nightmare of quietly lethal potency.
In Cooke’s taut, claustrophobic production, that scarcely matters: it still has the power to chill you to the bone.
Dominic Cooke ekes out the drama until it blooms into compelling psychological theatre with the feel of a fever dream.
Dominic Cooke’s stripped-back, almost abstract production implicates us all in a remorseless journey towards dehumanisation.
It was good, but not that good.
In the lead role, David Tennant is stonily cold and compassionless in his sink from goodness, but Dominic Cooke’s confused production needs more clarity for it to fly.
The play ultimately deals with individual choices and how far we will compromise our beliefs, values and principles in the face of threats to our own survival.
This sense of constant moral equivocation, of hypocrisy, and of the small compromises that allow evil to thrive, is what makes the play of ongoing universal significance.
It’s a strong framing, and there are striking, resonant messages within this work, but as drama it unsettles when really it should devastate.
Director Dominic Cooke has crafted a punchy first act, but he can’t save the second from Taylor’s stodgy script.

Tennant’s performance is terrifyingly magnificent; never missing a beat, Tennant keeps the audience enthralled, continually shocking us in the cool detachment with which he delivers some of the most chilling lines.

cn.t: Tennant delivers a magnetic, chilling performance in this timely but uneven revival of Taylor's Holocaust drama. Critics praise its urgent examination of moral compromise, though some find the production's stark approach mixed.
